questions.question: A gas molecule of mass m moves at speed v and strikes the side of a cylinder at an angle, taking time t to collide. Which gives the average force on the side of the cylinder?
questions.answer: D: 2 m v sin(theta) / t
steps: The angle theta is between the molecule's path and the wall, so the velocity component perpendicular to the wall is v sin(theta).
The component along the wall is unchanged, but the perpendicular component reverses: change in momentum = m v sin(theta) - (-m v sin(theta)) = 2 m v sin(theta).
Average force F = change in momentum / time = 2 m v sin(theta) / t.

questions.question: Momenta P and Q of two bodies about to merge are shown. Which diagram shows the resultant momentum after they move on as one body?
questions.answer: C
steps: Momentum is a vector, so the resultant is found by adding P and Q head to tail (tip to tail).
The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the second.
In diagram C, P and Q join head to tail and the resultant runs from the start of P to the end of Q. In A and B the arrows meet head to head; in D the resultant points the wrong way.

questions.question: A force of 14 N compresses a spring by 1.7 cm. Show that the maximum energy stored in the compressed spring is about 0.1 J.
questions.answer: E = 0.5 x 14 N x 0.017 m = 0.12 J, which is about 0.1 J.
steps: For a spring obeying Hooke's law, the energy stored is the work done in compressing it: E = area under F-x graph = (1/2) F x.
Convert the compression: x = 1.7 cm = 0.017 m.
This is about 0.1 J, as shown.

questions.question: Using the spring energy to find the maximum speed of the head (6.4 g) and the gravitational energy gained by the whole toy (7.2 g, max height 1.5 m) to find its initial upward speed, determine whether momentum is conserved.
questions.answer: Yes. The head at maximum speed has momentum 0.039 kg m s^-1, equal to the momentum of the whole toy (0.039 kg m s^-1) after it jumps, so momentum is conserved.
steps: Head speed from spring energy: (1/2) m_head v^2 = 0.119 J, so v = sqrt(2 x 0.119 / 0.0064) = 6.10 m s^-1.
Initial speed of whole toy from gravitational energy: m g h = (1/2) m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 1.5) = 5.42 m s^-1.
Momentum of head at maximum speed: 0.0064 kg x 6.10 m s^-1 = 0.039 kg m s^-1.
Momentum of whole toy after jumping: 0.0072 kg x 5.42 m s^-1 = 0.039 kg m s^-1.
The two momenta agree, so the toy obeys conservation of momentum (within rounding).

questions.question: Determine whether kinetic energy is conserved as the head starts to pull the base upwards.
questions.answer: No. KE falls from about 0.119 J to about 0.106 J, because the head and base join and move together (inelastic).
steps: Kinetic energy before the head pulls the base is that of the head: 0.119 J (from part (b)).
The head (6.10 m s^-1) joins the stationary base (0.8 g); momentum gives common speed v = 0.0064 x 6.10 / 0.0072 = 5.42 m s^-1.
KE falls from 0.119 J to 0.106 J, so kinetic energy is not conserved (the joined motion is inelastic).

questions.question: A ball of mass m with velocity v strikes a wall at right angles and rebounds at the same speed in the opposite direction. Which is the impulse on the wall? A mv; B 2mv; C -mv; D -2mv.
questions.answer: B - 2mv
steps: Ball momentum changes from +mv to -mv, a change of 2mv.
Impulse on the ball is -2mv, and by Newton's third law the impulse on the wall is equal and opposite.
The impulse on the wall is therefore 2mv in magnitude, directed into the wall.
Answer: B.

questions.question: A sphere of speed v collides elastically with an identical stationary sphere; after the collision both move off at the same angle to the original direction with equal speeds. What is the speed of the spheres after the collision?
questions.answer: v / sqrt(2) (each sphere moves at 45 degrees to the original direction)
steps: Kinetic energy is conserved (elastic): (1/2) m v^2 = 2 x (1/2) m u^2, so u^2 = v^2 / 2.
This gives u = v / sqrt(2).
Momentum along the original direction: m v = 2 m u cos(theta), so cos(theta) = v / (2u) = 1 / sqrt(2).
theta = 45 degrees, consistent with the symmetric outcome; the speed is v / sqrt(2).

questions.question: Sketch a labelled vector diagram showing the momenta of the spacecraft and asteroid before and after a collision at 90 degrees, where they remain joined.
questions.answer: A right-angled vector triangle: the large asteroid momentum and the small spacecraft momentum at 90 degrees, with the resultant momentum after the collision as the hypotenuse.
steps: Before: draw the asteroid momentum p_a as a long arrow and the spacecraft momentum p_s as a very short arrow at 90 degrees to it (label both).
Momentum is conserved, so after the collision the joined bodies have momentum equal to the vector sum of p_a and p_s.
Draw p_s from the tip of p_a (head to tail) and the resultant momentum from the tail of p_a to the tip of p_s, and label it "momentum after collision".
Mark the small angle between the resultant and the original asteroid direction (about 10^-7 rad, so the diagram must be exaggerated).

questions.question: Show that the momentum of a spacecraft of mass 920 kg moving at 12 000 m s^-1 is about 10^7 N s.
steps: Momentum p = m v.
This is about 10^7 N s, as shown.

questions.question: The asteroid has momentum 7.6 x 10^13 N s and the spacecraft momentum is about 10^7 N s, at 90 degrees. Show the asteroid's direction changes by about 10^-7 radian.
questions.answer: Angle = 1.45 x 10^-7 rad, which is about 10^-7 rad.
steps: The spacecraft's momentum is at 90 degrees to the asteroid's, so tan(theta) = p_spacecraft / p_asteroid.
For small angles tan(theta) is approximately theta in radians.
This is about 10^-7 rad, as shown.

questions.question: After the collision the asteroid (2.8 x 10^9 kg) and spacecraft (920 kg) move together. Calculate the velocity component at 90 degrees to the asteroid's original path.
questions.answer: Component of velocity = 3.9 x 10^-3 m s^-1
steps: Perpendicular momentum is conserved: the spacecraft's 1.10 x 10^7 N s is shared by the combined mass.
Combined mass = 2.8 x 10^9 kg + 920 kg = 2.80 x 10^9 kg.
Perpendicular velocity component = momentum / total mass = 1.10 x 10^7 / 2.80 x 10^9.

questions.question: A rocket motor applies a force of 5.1 x 10^6 N at 90 degrees to the asteroid's path for 6 minutes. Deduce whether this changes the momentum as much as the collision method.
questions.answer: Yes, much more. Impulse = 5.1 x 10^6 N x 360 s = 1.8 x 10^9 N s, compared with about 1.1 x 10^7 N s from the collision (about 170 times greater).
steps: Change in momentum = impulse = F t.
Time t = 6 min = 360 s, so impulse = 5.1 x 10^6 N x 360 s = 1.8 x 10^9 N s.
The collision changes the spacecraft momentum by about 1.1 x 10^7 N s (part b).
1.8 x 10^9 N s is about 170 times greater, so the rocket method produces a much greater change in momentum.

questions.question: A puck of mass 110 g reaches a speed of 0.35 m s^-1 after being pushed for 0.28 s. Using impulse, calculate the average force that accelerated it.
questions.answer: Average force = 0.14 N
steps: The puck starts from rest, so its change in momentum = m v = 0.110 kg x 0.35 m s^-1 = 0.0385 kg m s^-1.
Impulse = F t, so the average force F = change in momentum / time.
Average force = 0.14 N (to 2 s.f.).

questions.question: Puck 1 (110 g) moves at 0.41 m s^-1 and hits stationary puck 2 (130 g). Puck 1 moves off at 0.28 m s^-1 after the collision. Calculate the speed of puck 2 after the collision.
questions.answer: Speed of puck 2 = 0.26 m s^-1
steps: The pucks start along the horizontal, so the total momentum perpendicular to the original direction is zero after the collision. Puck 1 goes at 49 degrees above and puck 2 at 43 degrees below.
Perpendicular components: m1 v1 sin49 = m2 v2 sin43, so 0.110 x 0.28 x sin49 = 0.130 x v2 x sin43.
v2 = 0.26 m s^-1. (Check along the original direction: 0.110 x 0.28 cos49 + 0.130 x 0.262 cos43 = 0.0451 kg m s^-1, equal to the initial 0.110 x 0.41.)

questions.question: Deduce whether the collision between the two pucks described in part (b)(i) was elastic.
questions.answer: Not elastic: kinetic energy falls from 9.2 x 10^-3 J to 8.8 x 10^-3 J.
steps: An elastic collision conserves kinetic energy, so compare the total KE before and after.
The KE after is about 5% less than before, so some kinetic energy has been transferred to other forms and the collision was not perfectly elastic.

questions.question: Explain the assumption made when applying conservation of momentum to collisions.
questions.answer: No resultant external force acts on the system during the collision, so the system is isolated (friction and other external forces are negligible).
steps: Conservation of momentum applies to a closed system with no resultant external force.
In the puck experiment the air cushion removes friction, so no significant external horizontal force acts.
The collision forces between the pucks are internal, equal and opposite, and act for the same time.
So the assumption is that the net external impulse on the system during the collision is zero.

questions.question: A particle of mass m has kinetic energy Ek and momentum p. A second particle of mass 2m has kinetic energy 2Ek. Which is equal to the momentum of the second particle?
questions.answer: C: 2p
steps: For a non-relativistic particle Ek = p^2 / (2m), so p = sqrt(2 m Ek).
Second particle: p2 = sqrt(2 x 2m x 2Ek) = sqrt(8 m Ek) = 2 sqrt(2 m Ek).
So p2 = 2p.

questions.question: A particle of mass m has momentum p and kinetic energy Ek. A second particle of mass m/2 has momentum 2p. What is its kinetic energy? A Ek/8; B Ek/2; C 2Ek; D 8Ek.
questions.answer: D - 8 Ek
steps: Kinetic energy in terms of momentum: Ek = p^2 / (2m).
Second particle: Ek2 = (2p)^2 / (2 x m/2) = 4p^2 / m.
Since p^2 / m = 2 Ek, Ek2 = 4 x 2 Ek = 8 Ek.
Answer: D.

questions.question: Which row of a table identifies what happens to momentum and kinetic energy in an elastic collision?
questions.answer: A: momentum conserved, kinetic energy conserved
steps: Momentum is conserved in every collision when no external force acts.
In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved, so row A.

questions.question: Two trolleys X and Y (each 0.25 kg) collide and join with velocity 1 m s^-1 afterwards. Which is the kinetic energy of trolley X before the collision (A 0.5 J, B 1 J, C 2 J, D 4 J)?
steps: Trolley X has momentum p = 0.5 N s and mass 0.25 kg, so its speed is v = p / m = 0.5 / 0.25 = 2.0 m s^-1.

questions.question: Two trolleys X and Y (each 0.25 kg) join after colliding and move with velocity 1 m s^-1. Which row of the table is correct for this collision?
questions.answer: B: momentum conserved, inelastic collision
steps: Momentum before = 0.5 N s + 0 = 0.5 N s. After, the joined trolleys have mass 0.50 kg and speed 1 m s^-1: momentum = 0.50 N s, so momentum is conserved.
Kinetic energy has decreased, so the collision is inelastic. This is row B.

questions.question: An object of mass m has momentum p and kinetic energy E. Which is the mass of an object with momentum 2p and kinetic energy 4E?
questions.answer: B: m
steps: E = p^2 / 2m, so m = p^2 / 2E.
New object: m_new = (2p)^2 / (2 x 4E) = 4 p^2 / 8E = p^2 / 2E = m.

questions.question: Explain how a helicopter that moves air vertically downwards can maintain a constant height above the ground.
questions.answer: Blades push air downwards, giving it downward momentum; by Newton's third law the air pushes the helicopter up with a force equal to the rate of change of momentum of the air. When this lift equals its weight, the net force is zero and it hovers.
steps: The blades accelerate a large mass of air each second to a downward velocity, so the air gains downward momentum.
The rate of change of momentum of the air is a downward force on the air.
By Newton's third law the air exerts an equal upward force (thrust) on the helicopter.
When this upward thrust equals the weight, the resultant force is zero, so the helicopter stays at constant height (constant velocity, zero acceleration).

questions.question: A flyboard of total mass 175 kg hovers over the sea with a water jet pumped at 114 kg s^-1. Find the velocity of the water jet as it leaves, assuming negligible initial velocity.
questions.answer: Velocity of water jet = 15 m s^-1
steps: To hover at constant height, the upward force on the flyboard equals its weight: F = m g = 175 kg x 9.81 m s^-2 = 1717 N.
The force equals the rate of change of momentum of the water: F = (mass flow rate) x v.
v = F / (mass flow rate) = 1717 N / 114 kg s^-1 = 15.1 m s^-1.
Velocity of the water jet = 15 m s^-1.

questions.question: A collision between a white and a black snooker ball is inelastic. State what is meant by inelastic.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision; some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms (such as sound, heat or deformation).
steps: An elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy.
In an inelastic collision the total kinetic energy after the collision is less than before.
The lost kinetic energy goes into other forms such as sound, heat and deformation.
Momentum is still conserved in an inelastic collision.

questions.question: Explain why a scaled vector diagram of the velocities of the snooker balls can be used to demonstrate conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: Momentum is a vector, so the momentum vectors before the collision must sum to the same total as after; for equal masses the velocity vectors are proportional to momenta and form a closed triangle.
steps: Momentum is a vector quantity, so conservation requires the vector sum of momenta to be the same before and after.
The balls have equal masses, so their velocity vectors are proportional to their momentum vectors.
Before the collision only the white ball moves; after, the two velocity vectors should add to the original vector.
A scaled diagram that closes into a triangle therefore shows the vector sum is conserved.

questions.question: Using a scaled vector diagram, deduce whether the black ball moves towards the corner pocket shown in the figure.
questions.answer: Yes: the black ball leaves at about 50 degrees to the original direction, which is the direction of the pocket.
steps: Both balls have the same mass m, so the velocity vectors can be used in place of momentum vectors (the m cancels).
Draw the initial velocity of the white ball (1.20 m s^-1) to scale, then the white ball final velocity (0.92 m s^-1) at 35 degrees below the original line, from the same start point.
The black ball velocity completes the triangle (initial = white final + black final). The closing side measures about 0.69 m s^-1.
By calculation: x-component = 1.20 - 0.92 cos35 = 0.45 m s^-1; y-component = 0.92 sin35 = 0.53 m s^-1 (opposite side to the white ball).
Angle = tan^-1(0.53 / 0.45) = 50 degrees, which matches the 50 degrees line to the pocket, so the black ball moves towards the pocket.

questions.question: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: For a closed system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.
steps: Momentum is a vector, so the principle applies to the vector sum of momenta.
It applies to a system on which no resultant external force acts.
The total momentum before any interaction equals the total momentum after it.
Momentum is therefore constant (conserved) in the system.

questions.question: A spreadsheet modelled an elastic collision between objects A and B. Deduce from the initial and final values whether the collision was elastic.
questions.answer: No: total kinetic energy falls from 0.72 J to 0.66 J, so the values do not show an elastic collision.
steps: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is conserved.
Initial KE = 1/2 x 0.85 x 1.30^2 = 0.718 J (B is at rest).
The final KE is about 9% lower, a larger difference than rounding of the data would explain, so the collision is not elastic.

questions.question: Using the spreadsheet values for objects A and B, deduce whether they show conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: Yes: both components of momentum are conserved within rounding (x: 1.105 before, 1.098 after; y: 0 before, -0.004 after).
steps: Initial momentum (all along x): 0.85 x 1.30 = 1.105 kg m s^-1; y-component = 0.
The x-components differ by about 0.6% and the y-component is almost zero, so momentum is conserved within the precision of the data.

questions.question: An electron has kinetic energy 7.2 x 10^-16 J. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 1.8 x 10^-11 m
steps: Kinetic energy Ek = p^2 / (2m), so p = sqrt(2 m Ek).
de Broglie wavelength lambda = h / p = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s / 3.62 x 10^-23 kg m s^-1.
lambda = 1.8 x 10^-11 m.

questions.topic: Change In Momentum From Force And Time
questions.question: A drag force of 150 N acts on a car for 15 s. Which is the change in momentum of the car? A 10 kg m s^-1; B 1125 kg m s^-1; C 2250 kg m s^-1; D 16 875 kg m s^-1.
steps: Change in momentum = impulse = F x t.
Change in momentum = 150 N x 15 s = 2250 N s = 2250 kg m s^-1.
The magnitude is 2250 kg m s^-1, which matches option C.
Answer: C.

questions.question: Two 19.1 kg granite stones collide; one moves at 1.70 m s^-1 towards a stationary stone. Show that the speed v after the collision is about 1.3 m s^-1.
questions.answer: v = 1.33 m s^-1, which is about 1.3 m s^-1
steps: The stones have equal mass and the second stone is initially at rest. The momentum perpendicular to the original direction is zero before, so it is zero after.
Perpendicular components: 0.87 sin50 = v sin30.
Check along the original direction: 0.87 cos50 + 1.33 cos30 = 0.56 + 1.15 = 1.71, which agrees with the initial 1.70 m s^-1.

questions.question: Deduce whether the curling stone collision was elastic, including a calculation.
questions.answer: Not elastic: kinetic energy falls from 27.6 J to 24.2 J.
steps: KE after is less than KE before (about 12% less), so the collision is inelastic, not elastic.

questions.question: Which gives the base units of impulse? A kg m s^-1; B kg m s^-2; C N m; D N s.
questions.answer: A - kg m s^-1
steps: Impulse = F t, and force has base units kg m s^-2.
Impulse units = kg m s^-2 x s = kg m s^-1.
B is the unit of force (newton) and C is the unit of work (joule), so they are wrong.
D (N s) is an equivalent unit, not a base unit, so the answer is A.

questions.question: A ball of speed u hits a wall at right angles and bounces back at speed v in the opposite direction in collision time t. Which expression gives the average force on the wall?
questions.answer: A: m (u + v) / t
steps: Take the initial direction as positive: initial momentum = m u, final momentum = -m v.
Change in momentum of the ball = -m v - m u = -m (u + v), so its magnitude is m (u + v).
Average force = change in momentum / time = m (u + v) / t (on the wall, equal and opposite to the force on the ball).

questions.question: A non-relativistic particle of mass m has momentum p and kinetic energy Ek. A second non-relativistic particle has momentum 2p. Which expression gives its kinetic energy?
questions.answer: D: 8 Ek
steps: Ek = p^2 / 2m for a non-relativistic particle.
Second particle: mass m/2 and momentum 2p, so Ek2 = (2p)^2 / (2 x m/2) = 4 p^2 / m.
Compare with Ek = p^2 / 2m: Ek2 = 8 x p^2 / 2m = 8 Ek.

questions.question: A positive particle follows a circular path of radius 1.99 m in a magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity, with momentum 3.67 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1. Calculate B.
questions.answer: B = 1.15 T (about 1.2 T)
steps: Magnetic force provides the centripetal force: B q v = m v^2 / r, so p = m v = B q r.
Rearrange: B = p / (q r), taking the particle charge q = +e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C.

questions.question: The + particle is made of two up quarks and one strange quark. State what type of particle it is.
questions.answer: Baryon (a strange baryon, the Sigma-plus hyperon)
steps: The particle contains two up quarks and one strange quark: three quarks in total.
Particles made of three quarks are baryons (mesons contain a quark and an antiquark).
The uus combination with charge +1 is the Sigma-plus hyperon, which is a strange baryon.
Answer: baryon.

questions.question: Deduce whether conservation of charge and conservation of lepton number apply to the decay of the + particle into a + particle and a neutron (equation partly lost in the text).
questions.answer: Charge is conserved (+1 before, +1 + 0 after). Lepton number is conserved (zero before and after, since no leptons are involved).
steps: Taking the decay as Sigma-plus -> pi-plus + neutron (the three particles shown in part (iii)).
Charge before = +1; charge after = +1 (pi-plus) + 0 (neutron) = +1, so charge is conserved.
No leptons appear on either side of the decay, so the lepton number is 0 before and after.
Both charge and lepton number are conserved in this decay.

questions.question: Using the directions of the three particles at the decay, determine the magnitude and direction of the neutron's momentum, given the + particle momentum 3.67 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1 and pion momentum 1.07 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1.
questions.answer: Magnitude of neutron momentum = 3.4 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1; direction 17 degrees to the original direction of the Sigma-plus (on the opposite side to the pion).
steps: Momentum is conserved in both directions. Take the original direction of the Sigma-plus as the vertical axis.
Perpendicular to the original direction (horizontal): p_n sin(theta) = p_pion sin65 = 1.07 x 10^-19 x 0.906 = 9.7 x 10^-20 kg m s^-1.
Along the original direction (vertical): p_n cos(theta) = 3.67 x 10^-19 - 1.07 x 10^-19 x cos65 = 3.67 x 10^-19 - 4.5 x 10^-20 = 3.22 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1.
tan(theta) = 9.7 x 10^-20 / 3.22 x 10^-19 = 0.30, so theta = 17 degrees to the original direction, on the opposite side from the pion.

questions.question: Add to the bubble chamber diagram all tracks visible after the decay at X, and label the diagram.
questions.answer: Add one curved track from X for the positively charged pion, with a smaller radius than the sigma track; no track for the neutral neutron.
steps: The pion (pi-plus) is charged, so it ionises the liquid and leaves a visible track starting at X, in the direction of its momentum (65 degrees from the sigma direction, on the opposite side to the neutron).
It has the same charge sign as the sigma, so it curves in the same sense in the magnetic field.
Its momentum is smaller (1.07 x 10^-19 compared with 3.67 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1), so r = p / (B q) is about 0.58 m, much smaller than 1.99 m: the track is more tightly curved.
The neutron is neutral and does not ionise, so no track is drawn for it (it may be labelled "neutron: no track"). Label the incoming track Sigma-plus and the new track pi-plus.

questions.question: Explain how using the air table ensured that momentum was conserved in collisions between the pucks.
questions.answer: The air cushion removes friction, so no significant external horizontal force acts on the pucks; the collision forces are internal, so the total momentum of the pucks is conserved.
steps: The air blown through the holes lifts the pucks on a cushion of air.
This removes friction between the pucks and the table surface.
With no significant external horizontal force, the pucks form a closed system.
Collision forces are internal and equal and opposite, so the total momentum of the pucks is conserved.

questions.question: Two identical pucks A and B collide with one puck initially stationary, and their paths after collision are at 90 degrees. Deduce using conservation of momentum whether the angle is 90 degrees.
questions.answer: Yes: a + b = 33 + 58 = 91 degrees, which is about 90 degrees.
steps: Puck B is initially stationary and the pucks have equal mass; B must gain momentum equal to the missing momentum of A.
Perpendicular to the original direction: p_B sin(b) = p_A sin33 = 0.039 x 0.545 = 0.0212 kg m s^-1.
Along the original direction: p_B cos(b) = 0.046 - 0.039 cos33 = 0.046 - 0.0327 = 0.0133 kg m s^-1.
The angle between the paths is a + b = 33 + 58 = 91 degrees, which is 90 degrees within the precision of the data.

questions.topic: Elastic Test For Air Table Pucks
questions.question: Deduce whether the collision between the identical pucks (mass 0.110 kg each) was elastic, using the recorded data.
questions.answer: Elastic: KE after = 9.8 x 10^-3 J, equal to KE before = 9.6 x 10^-3 J within about 2%.
steps: Use Ek = p^2 / 2m with m = 0.110 kg.
The totals agree within the rounding of the data (about 2%), so the collision was elastic.

questions.question: Explain the quark structure of a K- meson, a strange particle with charge -1.
questions.answer: K- = strange quark plus anti-up quark (s u-bar); charges -1/3 + (-2/3) = -1.
steps: The K- meson has charge -1 e and is strange.
Strangeness -1 requires an anti-strange or strange quark with negative strangeness; the strange quark s has charge -1/3.
An anti-up quark u-bar has charge -2/3, giving a total charge of -1/3 + (-2/3) = -1.
So the K- meson is made of one strange quark and one anti-up quark (s u-bar).

questions.question: The K- meson has mass 494 MeV/c^2. Calculate its mass in kg.
questions.answer: Mass = 8.8 x 10^-28 kg
steps: Mass from E = m c^2, so m = E / c^2.

questions.question: Explain how a cyclotron produces a beam of high-energy particles, referring to the alternating pd and the magnetic field.
questions.answer: The magnetic field makes particles move in circles, while the alternating pd across the gap, synchronised with the orbit frequency, accelerates them each time they cross. Their radius grows until they exit with high energy.
steps: Particles are injected near the centre of two D-shaped electrodes in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane.
The magnetic force acts at right angles to the velocity, so the particles follow circular paths.
The alternating pd across the gap between the electrodes is set to the orbital frequency f = qB / (2 pi m), so it accelerates the particles each time they cross the gap.
Each acceleration increases the speed and radius, so the particles spiral outwards and leave the cyclotron with high kinetic energy.

questions.question: A 1929 cyclotron (diameter 0.11 m) gave protons a maximum kinetic energy of 80 keV. Calculate the magnetic flux density of the field.
steps: Radius r = diameter / 2 = 0.055 m; kinetic energy Ek = 80 x 10^3 eV = 80 000 x 1.60 x 10^-19 J = 1.28 x 10^-14 J.
Momentum from Ek: p = sqrt(2 m Ek), with proton mass m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg (data booklet): p = sqrt(2 x 1.67 x 10^-27 x 1.28 x 10^-14) = 6.54 x 10^-21 kg m s^-1.
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so p = B q r and B = p / (q r).

questions.question: A helium atom of mass m and velocity v collides at right angles with a surface and rebounds with the same speed in the opposite direction in time t. Which is the mean force on the atom?
questions.answer: D: -2 m v / delta t
steps: Take the initial direction of motion (towards the surface, as shown by the arrow) as positive. Initial momentum = m v, final momentum = -m v.
Change in momentum of the atom = -m v - m v = -2 m v.
Mean force on the atom = change in momentum / delta t = -2 m v / delta t (negative: directed away from the surface).

questions.question: For a force-time graph of a ball bouncing off a wall, which is given by the area under the graph? A acceleration of the ball; B average force on the ball; C change in momentum of the ball; D distance travelled by the ball.
questions.answer: C - change in momentum of the ball
steps: Force F against time t: the area under the graph is the integral of F dt.
This integral is the impulse, which equals the change in momentum.
Average force and acceleration are not given by an area, and distance is not a force-time quantity.
Answer: C.

questions.question: State what is meant by the principle of conservation of momentum.
questions.answer: The total momentum of a system is constant (the same before and after an interaction) provided no resultant external force acts on the system.
steps: Momentum is a vector; the principle concerns the total vector momentum of a system.
The principle applies when no resultant external force acts on the system (a closed system).
The total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it.
So the total momentum of the system stays constant.

questions.question: An alpha particle collides with a stationary helium nucleus at X; the alpha particle moves off at 20 degrees to its original direction with speed 1.55 x 10^7 m s^-1. Show the helium nucleus speed after collision is about 5.6 x 10^6 m s^-1 (mass 6.64 x 10^-27 kg; initial alpha KE 9.01 x 10^-13 J from part (ii)).
questions.answer: v(helium) = 5.6 x 10^6 m s^-1
steps: Initial alpha speed from KE: v0 = sqrt(2 Ek / m) = sqrt(2 x 9.01 x 10^-13 / 6.64 x 10^-27) = 1.65 x 10^7 m s^-1 (the nucleus is at rest before).
Initial momentum p0 = m v0 = 6.64 x 10^-27 x 1.65 x 10^7 = 1.09 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1 along the original direction.
Alpha momentum after: p1 = m x 1.55 x 10^7 = 1.03 x 10^-19 kg m s^-1 at 20 degrees; components (9.67 x 10^-20, 3.52 x 10^-20).
Helium momentum p2 = p0 - p1 = (1.27 x 10^-20, -3.52 x 10^-20), magnitude 3.74 x 10^-20 kg m s^-1, so v = p2 / m = 5.6 x 10^6 m s^-1.

questions.question: The alpha particle's kinetic energy before collision was 9.01 x 10^-13 J. Deduce whether the collision was elastic.
questions.answer: Elastic: total KE after is about 9.03 x 10^-13 J, which matches the 9.01 x 10^-13 J before within rounding.
steps: KE before = 9.01 x 10^-13 J (given).
KE of helium nucleus after = (1/2) x 6.64 x 10^-27 kg x (5.6 x 10^6 m s^-1)^2 = 1.05 x 10^-13 J.
Total KE after = 9.03 x 10^-13 J, equal to 9.01 x 10^-13 J within rounding, so the collision is elastic.

questions.topic: Accelerating Pd From de Broglie Wavelength
questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron beam in a diffraction tube is 2.55 x 10^-11 m. Calculate the accelerating pd V.
steps: Momentum from wavelength: p = h / lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s / 2.55 x 10^-11 m = 2.60 x 10^-23 kg m s^-1.
The electron is accelerated from rest through pd V, so e V = Ek.

questions.question: An electron has kinetic energy 3.5 x 10^-28 J. Which gives its momentum in kg m s^-1?
steps: For a non-relativistic particle Ek = p^2 / 2m, so p = sqrt(2 m Ek).
The value is about 2.5 x 10^-29 kg m s^-1.

questions.topic: Momentum And KE In Inelastic Collision
questions.question: A moving trolley collides with a stationary trolley and they move off together, with negligible friction and an inelastic collision. Which row of the table shows the change in total momentum and total kinetic energy?
questions.answer: B: total momentum conserved; total kinetic energy not conserved (decreases)
steps: Frictional forces are negligible, so no resultant external force acts and the total momentum is conserved.
The collision is inelastic and the trolleys stick together, so some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms (heat, sound), and the total kinetic energy decreases. This is row B.

questions.question: Explain why a thick rubber strip around each car reduces the likelihood of injury to drivers when two cars collide and stop, referring to change in momentum.
questions.answer: The change in momentum is the same, but the rubber lengthens the collision time, so the average force (rate of change of momentum) on the drivers is smaller.
steps: Both cars come to rest, so the change in momentum of each car is the same with or without the strip.
Force F = change in momentum / time (F = Delta p / Delta t).
The rubber strip increases the time over which the cars stop.
A longer time gives a smaller average force on the drivers, so the likelihood of injury is reduced.

questions.question: Car A (390 kg) moves at 2.19 m s^-1 and hits stationary car B (360 kg). After the collision A moves at 1.21 m s^-1 at 48 degrees to its original direction, and B moves at angle 33 degrees. Deduce whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.
questions.answer: Inelastic. KE before is about 935 J, KE after is about 860 J.
steps: Momentum before = 390 kg x 2.19 m s^-1 = 854 kg m s^-1 along the original direction.
x-direction: 390 x 1.21 cos48 + 360 v cos33 = 854, so 360 v cos33 = 538 and v cos33 = 1.50 m s^-1.
y-direction: 390 x 1.21 sin48 = 360 v sin33, so v = 1.79 m s^-1 (consistent with the x-result).
KE after is less than KE before, so the collision is inelastic.

questions.question: In nuclear fission a nucleus splits into nucleus S, nucleus T and neutrons. S and T have the same kinetic energy and T has twice the mass of S. Which is the ratio shown in the missing expression?
questions.answer: C: square root of 2
steps: For a non-relativistic particle Ek = p^2 / 2m, so p = sqrt(2 m Ek).
S and T have the same Ek, so p is proportional to sqrt(m).
p_T / p_S = sqrt(m_T / m_S) = sqrt(2).

questions.question: A sphere of mass 35 g rolls into two stationary spheres of mass 37 g each; the rolling sphere stops and the two spheres move apart at an angle theta. Determine the angle theta, assuming the collision is elastic.
questions.answer: theta = 47 degrees (cos^2(theta) = 35/74)
steps: Assume the collision is elastic (kinetic energy conserved), as needed to fix the angle.
Momentum along the original direction: 35 u = 2 x 37 v cos(theta).
Kinetic energy: (1/2) x 35 u^2 = 2 x (1/2) x 37 v^2, so 35 u^2 = 74 v^2.
Substituting v = 35 u / (74 cos theta) gives cos^2(theta) = 35/74 = 0.473, so cos(theta) = 0.688 and theta = 47 degrees.

questions.question: Explain why electrons are released when there is a current in the filament of a cathode ray tube.
questions.answer: The current heats the filament, giving electrons enough thermal energy to escape from the surface of the metal (thermionic emission).
steps: The current through the filament heats it.
Heating gives conduction electrons kinetic energy.
Electrons with enough energy to overcome the work function escape from the surface of the filament.
This emission of electrons is thermionic emission.

questions.question: Electrons in a cathode ray tube have de Broglie wavelength 2.65 x 10^-11 m. Calculate the pd V needed to accelerate them.
steps: Momentum p = h / lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s / 2.65 x 10^-11 m = 2.50 x 10^-23 kg m s^-1.
Electrons accelerated from rest through pd V gain Ek = e V.
